finding.claim: /fetch2 makes an arbitrary server-side GET to any attacker-supplied URL. The only check is the scheme (http/https). Internal hosts such as 127.0.0.1, RFC1918 addresses, and 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata are reachable. Redirects are followed (requests default), so even a stricter check could be bypassed by a 3xx to an internal host. The first 200 characters of the response body are returned to the caller, so the response is readable (non-blind SSRF).
finding.sink: views.py:22 requests.get(url, timeout=5) with default allow_redirects=True; response returned via views.py:22 jsonify body[:200]

trace.note: is_http_url: returns urlparse(url).scheme in ("http","https"); no host/IP check
requests.get(url, timeout=5) with redirects enabled, body reflected to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Scheme allowlist only (validators.py:7). No hostname, IP, or private-range check, no DNS resolution check, no port restriction, redirects not disabled, no auth on route. Not sufficient.

verdict.guard_found: Only is_http_url at views.py:20 (validators.py:6-7), a scheme-only check. The stronger is_safe_url (validators.py:10-18, which blocks private/loopback/link-local/reserved IPs and disables redirects at views.py:14) is applied only to /fetch at views.py:12, not to /fetch2. No hostname, IP, or redirect guard exists on the /fetch2 path.
verdict.reason: The candidate's trace matches the code: the unauthenticated route at views.py:17 takes url from request.args at views.py:19, the only guard at views.py:20 is the scheme-only is_http_url (validators.py:7), and views.py:22 issues requests.get with default redirects and returns body[:200] to the caller. The stricter is_safe_url used by /fetch at views.py:12 is not applied to /fetch2, so the finding stands.

finding.claim: /fetch validates the destination IP and then fetches a URL that is resolved again. An attacker-controlled DNS name can return a public IP to is_safe_url and a private/loopback/metadata IP (e.g. 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1) to requests.get. This is a DNS rebinding TOCTOU bypass of the SSRF guard.
finding.source: views.py:11 request.args.get("url") with a hostname the attacker controls DNS for
finding.sink: views.py:14 requests.get(url) - performs its own DNS resolution, separate from the check at validators.py:14

trace.note: socket.getaddrinfo(parsed.hostname, ...) - first resolution; attacker DNS returns public IP here
ip checked against private/loopback/link_local/reserved - passes for public IP
requests.get(url) - second, independent DNS resolution (urllib3); attacker DNS now returns internal IP, connection made to it

finding.guards_checked: is_safe_url scheme and hostname presence (validators.py:12); IP range checks on all getaddrinfo results (validators.py:14-17); allow_redirects=False (views.py:14) blocks the redirect-based bypass, so the rebinding is the remaining path. Check is not pinned to the connected IP. Not sufficient.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is is_safe_url at views.py:12, which validates scheme and hostname presence (validators.py:12) and then checks resolved IPs against private/loopback/link_local/reserved ranges (validators.py:14-17). That is not an exact hostname allowlist, anchored match, or scheme-plus-host membership. The IP check is not pinned to the IP that requests.get connects to (views.py:14), so it does not close the rebinding path. allow_redirects=False at views.py:14 only blocks redirects, not DNS rebinding.
verdict.reason: The source is the unauthenticated query parameter `url` (views.py:11), and every trace line matches the file: is_safe_url resolves the hostname via getaddrinfo (validators.py:14) and rejects private/loopback/link-local/reserved results (validators.py:16-17), and then requests.get(url) at views.py:14 performs an independent DNS resolution with no pinned IP. Nothing closes this path, so an attacker-controlled DNS name that returns a public IP on the check and an internal IP on the fetch bypasses the guard. Exploitability depends on the attacker's DNS answering differently on the second lookup (low TTL or a rebinding server), so it is a real TOCTOU rather than a guaranteed one-shot bypass.

finding.claim: The is_safe_url blocklist does not cover the carrier-grade NAT range 100.64.0.0/10. Python's ipaddress reports is_private/is_loopback/is_link_local/is_reserved as False for it, so it passes. This range includes 100.100.100.200, the Alibaba Cloud instance metadata endpoint, so on Alibaba-hosted deployments the /fetch route can reach metadata. Exploitability depends on hosting, and this was not verified by execution.

trace.note: getaddrinfo resolves hostname to 100.100.100.200 (IP literal works too)
is_private/loopback/link_local/reserved are all False for 100.64.0.0/10, so the check does not block

finding.guards_checked: Blocklist in validators.py:16 is missing 100.64.0.0/10. Redirects are disabled (views.py:14). The check is otherwise sound for 127/8, 169.254/16, RFC1918, and fc00::/7.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:12 calls is_safe_url, but validators.py:16 checks only is_private, is_loopback, is_link_local, and is_reserved, and none of these is True for 100.64.0.0/10 (CGNAT). The only other protections are redirects disabled at views.py:14 and a 5s timeout, neither of which closes the range.
verdict.reason: The source is the attacker-supplied query parameter at views.py:11, and is_safe_url (validators.py:10-18) does not exclude 100.64.0.0/10, so a request to 100.100.100.200 passes the check and views.py:14 issues requests.get to it. Impact on Alibaba-hosted deployments depends on hosting, which I did not verify by execution; the validator's gap itself is confirmed by reading the code.
